reports.text: ARCHIVE: Israel did not start the campaign for the Iraq war. The neoconservatives did. But once Israel saw that Bush was serious, Israeli leaders joined in and pushed hard. And when a diplomatic path opened through UN inspections, they worked to close it. April 2002: Benjamin Netanyahu came to Washington. He met US senators and the editors of the Washington Post. He warned them that Saddam was developing nuclear weapons that could be delivered against the American homeland in suitcases or satchels. A few weeks later Ra'anan Gissen, Sharon spokesman, told a Cleveland reporter: "If Saddam Hussein is not stopped now, five years from now, six years from now, we will have to deal with an Iraq that is armed with nuclear weapons, with an Iraq that has delivery systems for weapons of mass destruction." Mid-May: Shimon Peres appeared on CNN. "Saddam Hussein is as dangerous as bin Laden," he said. The United States "cannot sit and wait" while he builds a nuclear arsenal. June: Ehud Barak wrote an op-ed in the Washington Post. He recommended the Bush administration "should, first of all, focus on Iraq and the removal of Saddam Hussein. Once he is gone there will be a different Arab world." August 12: Sharon told the Knesset Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee that Iraq "is the greatest danger facing Israel." August 16, ten days before Cheney kicked off the war campaign with his VFW speech: Ha'aretz, the Washington Post, CNN, and CBS all reported that Israel was urging the US not to delay the attack. Sharon told the Bush administration that postponing "will not create a more convenient environment for action in the future." Peres told CNN "the problem today is not if, but when." Deputy Defense Minister Weizman Shiry said: "If the Americans do not do this now, it will be harder to do it in the future." CBS headline: "Israel to US: Don't Delay Iraq Attack." Peres and Sharon made sure to say they did not want to be seen as pushing America. But their public comments show the opposite. Then the inspections path opened. September 2002: Bush decided to seek UN Security Council authorization for war. Israelis were distressed. Then Saddam agreed to let UN inspectors back in. They were more worried still. Peres told reporters: "The campaign against Saddam Hussein is a must. Inspections and inspectors are good for decent people, but dishonest people can overcome easily inspections and inspectors." Sharon flew to Moscow in late September. He told Vladimir Putin, who was leading the charge for new inspections, that it was too late for them to be effective. Peres got so frustrated with the UN process that in mid-February 2003 he lashed out at France and questioned its status as a permanent member of the Security Council. Marc Perelman wrote in the Forward in mid-September 2002: "Saddam Hussein surprise acceptance of unconditional United Nations weapons inspections put Israel on the hot seat this week, forcing it into the open as the only nation actively supporting the Bush administration goal of Iraqi regime change." Israeli figures compared Saddam to Hitler and called opponents of the war appeasers. Shlomo Avineri wrote in the Los Angeles Times: "all who condemn the 1930s appeasement of Germany should reflect long and hard on whether a failure to act today against Iraq will one day be viewed the same way." The Jerusalem Post editorialized that "ousting Saddam is the linchpin of the war on terrorism, without which it is impossible to begin in earnest, let alone win." My analysis is look at the sequence. When there was no diplomatic path, Israel pushed for war. When the UN inspections path opened, Israel said inspections are useless. When France tried to keep that path alive, Peres attacked France. They did not want inspections. They did not want a deal. They wanted the war. And when it happened, they said they never pushed for it. The public record says otherwise. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: Israel was not just pushing for war. It was feeding Washington intelligence about Iraq WMD that later turned out to be false. Around August 2002 news stories reported that "Israeli intelligence officials have gathered evidence that Iraq is speeding up efforts to produce biological and chemical weapons." Peres told CNN that "we think and know that he [Saddam] is on his way to acquiring a nuclear option." Ha'aretz reported that Saddam had given an "order... to Iraq's Atomic Energy Commission last week to speed up its work." Israel was feeding these alarming reports to Washington at a time when, in Sharon own words, "strategic coordination between Israel and the U.S. has reached unprecedented dimensions." Then the invasion happened. No WMD were found. The Senate Intelligence Committee and the Israeli Knesset both released separate reports afterward. Both revealed that much of the intelligence Israel gave to the Bush administration was false. As one retired Israeli general put it: "Israeli intelligence was a full partner to the picture presented by American and British intelligence regarding Iraq's non-conventional capabilities." So the same country pushing for the war was also the source of the false intelligence used to sell the war. That is not two separate stories. That is one story. My analysis is this is the part that should end the debate. People say Bush lied. Maybe he did. But who fed him the lies? The Senate and the Knesset both did reports. Both found the same thing. Israeli intelligence was false and it was a full partner in the case for war. Then after the war turned into a disaster, Israel said it never pushed for the war. The Knesset report says otherwise. So does Sharon own spokesman. So does Peres on CNN. So does the retired general. They cannot have it both ways. They supplied the lies and then they walked away from the result. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: Israel was the only country outside the United States, apart from Kuwait, where a majority of politicians and the public enthusiastically favored the Iraq war. A poll taken in early 2002 found that 58 percent of Israeli Jews believed that "Israel should encourage the United States to attack Iraq." Another poll taken a year later, in February 2003, found that 77.5 percent of Israeli Jews wanted the United States to invade Iraq. Compare that to Britain, America closest ally. A poll taken just before the war found that 51 percent of Britons opposed it, while only 39 percent supported it. In Britain 50,000 people demonstrated against the war. In Israel nobody did. Gideon Levy of Ha'aretz asked why. "Why is it that in Israel there is no public debate about whether the war is necessary?" His answer: "Israel is the only country in the West whose leaders support the war unreservedly and where no alternative opinion is voiced." Ha'aretz ran a story in February 2003 titled "Enthusiastic IDF Awaits War in Iraq." It said Israel "military and political leadership yearns for war in Iraq." The Forward ran a piece titled "Jerusalem Frets as U.S. Battles Iraq War Delays." Israel leaders wanted the war sooner, not later. Bill Clinton said in 2006 that "every Israeli politician I knew" believed Saddam was such a threat that he should be removed even if he did not have WMD. But here is the part that matters. Israel did not want Americans to know this. In fall 2002 a group of American political consultants called the Israel Project circulated a six-page memo to key Israelis and pro-Israel leaders in the US. It was titled "Talking about Iraq." It told them: "If your goal is regime change, you must be much more careful with your language because of the potential backlash. You do not want Americans to believe that the war on Iraq is being waged to protect Israel rather than to protect America." Sharon told Israeli diplomats and politicians to keep quiet about a possible war. He was worried by the growing perception that Israel was advocating a US invasion. In fact Israel was advocating it. It just did not want its position to be widely known. My analysis is this is the whole playbook in one chapter. Push the war in private. Sell the threat in public. Then when Americans start to notice, send a memo saying dont let them think it is for Israel. And tell your own diplomats to shut up. That is not a country with nothing to hide. That is a country that knows exactly what it is doing and knows it cannot say it out loud. The 77.5 percent wanted the war. The memo told them to hide it. Both are on the record. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: The people who pushed the Iraq war inside the Bush administration were not random. Many of them had documented ties to Israel and to pro-Israel groups. And one of them coauthored a report that said removing Saddam was an Israeli objective. Douglas Feith was the number three civilian at the Pentagon. Richard Perle chaired the Defense Policy Board. David Wurmser worked for John Bolton at the State Department. In June 1996 the three of them coauthored a report called "A Clean Break: A New Strategy for Securing the Realm." It was written for incoming Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The report recommended that Netanyahu "focus on removing Saddam Hussein from power in Iraq—an important Israeli strategic objective in its own right." It also called for Israel to reorder the entire Middle East. Netanyahu did not implement their advice. But Feith, Perle, and Wurmser were soon advocating the same goals inside the Bush administration. The Ha'aretz columnist Akiva Eldar warned that Feith and Perle "are walking a fine line between their loyalty to American governments and Israeli interests." George Packer wrote in The Assassins' Gate that "for Feith and Wurmser, the security of Israel was probably the prime mover" behind their support for the war. Paul Wolfowitz was deputy defense secretary. When he was selected in January 2001 the Jerusalem Post reported that "the Jewish and pro-Israel communities are jumping with joy." The Forward called him "the most hawkishly pro-Israel voice in the Administration." He received an award from JINSA for promoting a strong Israel-US partnership, and the Jerusalem Post named him its "Man of the Year" in 2003. John Bolton was undersecretary of state. As ambassador to the UN he consistently defended Israel interests. In May 2006 the Israeli ambassador to the UN jokingly described Bolton as "a secret member of Israel's own team at the United Nations." He added: "The secret is out. We really are not just five diplomats. We are at least six including John Bolton." Scooter Libby was the vice president chief of staff. The Forward reported when he left the White House that "Israeli officials liked Libby. They described him as an important contact who was accessible, genuinely interested in Israel-related issues and very sympathetic to their cause." Not all the war hawks were Jewish. James Woolsey, former CIA director, was obsessed with proving Saddam was behind 9/11. He pushed an implausible story that hijacker Mohammed Atta met an Iraqi intelligence agent in Prague. The story is widely believed to be false. Woolsey and Cheney both used it to sell the war. the Clean Break report is the smoking gun. 1996. Written for Netanyahu. By the same people who ran the Pentagon and the Defense Policy Board in 2003. It literally says removing Saddam is "an important Israeli strategic objective in its own right." Seven years later they got it done using American soldiers and American money. And the Israeli ambassador to the UN later joked that Bolton was a secret member of Israel team. That is not a conspiracy theory. That is a joke told in public by the Israeli ambassador himself. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: The neoconservatives were not just determined. They were obsessed. And almost nobody else in the government wanted this war. September 15 2001, four days after 9/11. Bush met with his team at Camp David. Paul Wolfowitz advocated attacking Iraq before Afghanistan. There was no evidence Saddam was involved in 9/11. Bin Laden was known to be in Afghanistan. Wolfowitz pushed Iraq anyway. Five days later Cheney had to tell him to "stop agitating for targeting Saddam." One Republican lawmaker said Wolfowitz "was like a parrot bringing Iraq up all the time. It was getting on the President nerves." Robert Kagan later said: "September 11 is the turning point. Not anything else. This is not what Bush was on September 10." Before 9/11 neither Bush nor Cheney was pushing for war. Cheney had spent the 1990s saying conquering Iraq would be a strategic blunder. He did not sign either of the 1998 neocon letters to Clinton calling for Saddam removal. In the 2000 campaign Bush did not advocate force against Saddam. His main foreign policy adviser Condoleezza Rice wrote in Foreign Affairs in early 2000 that the US could live with a nuclear-armed Iraq. She said Saddam conventional military power had been "severely weakened" and "there need be no sense of panic." Once 9/11 happened the neocons had their opening. And they were alone. There was little enthusiasm for the Iraq war in the State Department, the intelligence community, or the uniformed military. Colin Powell believed the war was a bad idea. The rank and file in his department agreed. George Tenet at the CIA supported the White House but was not a forceful advocate. General Eric Shinseki, the army chief of staff, was publicly attacked by Wolfowitz for saying the occupation would need more troops. Wolfowitz called his estimate "wildly off the mark." A senior administration figure said in January 2003: "I do believe certain people have grown theological about this. It is almost a religion—that it will be the end of our society if we dont take action now." A Washington Post journalist described Colin Powell coming out of White House meetings, rolling his eyes and saying: "Jeez, what a fixation about Iraq." The war hawks were mainly high-level civilians in the White House and the Pentagon. Almost all of them were neoconservatives. Richard Perle said it himself to George Packer. "If Bush had staffed his administration with a group of people selected by Brent Scowcroft and Jim Baker, which might well have happened, then it could have been different, because they would not have carried into it the ideas that the people who wound up in important positions brought to it." Thomas Friedman said in May 2003: "I could give you the names of 25 people (all of whom are at the moment within a five-block radius of this office), who, if you exiled them to a desert island a year and a half ago, the Iraq war would not have happened." the neocons did not represent America. They did not even represent the US government. Powell thought it was a bad idea. The CIA was skeptical. The army was skeptical. Shinseki got attacked for telling the truth about troop numbers. Twenty-five people inside a five-block radius in Washington. That is how a war that killed hundreds of thousands of people got started. Not because America wanted it. Because a small group of people with a foreign policy agenda captured the moment after 9/11. Perle admitted it. Friedman said it out loud. They are telling us who did it. We should listen. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: When the CIA and the intelligence community would not give the neocons the WMD evidence they wanted, they built their own intelligence operations. And one of them had a direct line to Ariel Sharon office. Scooter Libby, the vice president chief of staff, visited the CIA several times to pressure analysts to find evidence for the war. According to Bob Woodward, Powell deputy Richard Armitage "was appalled at what he considered overreaching and hyperbole. Libby was drawing only the worst conclusions from fragments and silky threads." Douglas Feith at the Pentagon set up two offices after 9/11. The first was the Policy Counterterrorism Evaluation Group. It was tasked to find links between al Qaeda and Iraq that the intelligence community supposedly missed. Its two key members were David Wurmser and Michael Maloof, a Lebanese American with close ties to Richard Perle. The New York Times reporter James Risen wrote that "Israeli intelligence played a hidden role in convincing Wolfowitz that he couldnt trust the CIA." The second was the Office of Special Plans. It was directed to find evidence to sell the war. It was headed by Abram Shulsky, a neoconservative close to Wolfowitz. Its staff included recruits from pro-Israel think tanks, including Michael Rubin from the American Enterprise Institute and Michael Makovsky, who had worked for Shimon Peres. Here is the part that matters most. The Guardian reported that the Office of Special Plans "forged close ties to a parallel, ad hoc intelligence operation inside Ariel Sharon office in Israel specifically to bypass Mossad and provide the Bush administration with more alarmist reports on Saddam Iraq than Mossad was prepared to authorize." So the Pentagon built its own intelligence shop. That shop worked directly with a secret operation inside the Israeli prime minister office. The purpose was to bypass Israel own intelligence agency because Mossad was not giving them the alarmist reports they wanted. Then those reports went into the case for war. The Department of Defense inspector general released a report in February 2007 critical of the Office of Special Plans for disseminating "alternative intelligence assessments" that were "in our opinion, inappropriate given that the intelligence assessments were intelligence products and did not clearly show the variance with the consensus of the Intelligence Community." The neocons also relied on Ahmed Chalabi and the Iraqi National Congress for intelligence. Chalabi had close ties to JINSA, AIPAC, AEI, the Hudson Institute, and WINEP. He was a frequent guest at JINSA board meetings since 1997. In return for the lobby support, Chalabi promised to foster good relations with Israel once he gained power. According to Feith former law partner L. Marc Zell, Chalabi also promised to rebuild the pipeline that once ran from Haifa in Israel to Mosul in Iraq. The CIA and State Department considered Chalabi dishonest and kept him at arm length. They were right. Chalabi and the INC fed the United States false information. they did not just cherry-pick intelligence. They built a whole separate intelligence agency to produce the intelligence they wanted. And that agency worked with a secret office inside the Israeli prime minister office, bypassing Mossad because Mossad would not give them the scary stories they needed. That is not a mistake. That is not a failure of intelligence. That is manufacturing intelligence. Then they leaked it to friendly journalists and called it proof. And when it all fell apart, nobody was punished. The inspector general report came out in 2007 and nothing happened. Because by then the war was already sold. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: The pro-Israel organizations were among the strongest supporters of the Iraq war. But the wider American Jewish community was against it. That gap is the whole point. Michelle Goldberg wrote in Salon in mid-September 2002: "mainstream Jewish groups and leaders are now among the strongest supporters of an American invasion of Baghdad." A Forward editorial after Baghdad fell put it plainly: "As President Bush attempted to sell the war in Iraq, America most important Jewish organizations rallied as one to his defense. In statement after statement community leaders stressed the need to rid the world of Saddam Hussein and his weapons of mass destruction." The editorial added: "concern for Israel safety rightfully factored into the deliberations of the main Jewish groups." In fall 2002 the Jewish Council for Public Affairs and the Conference of Presidents of Major American Jewish Organizations voted to support the use of force against Iraq "as a last resort." Mortimer Zuckerman chaired the Conference of Presidents and edited U.S. News & World Report. He wrote in late August 2002: "The best medicine here, in other words, is preventive medicine." Rabbi David Saperstein headed the Religious Action Center of Reform Judaism. The Washington Post called him "the quintessential religious lobbyist on Capitol Hill." He said in September 2002 that "the Jewish Community would want to see a forceful resolution to the threat that Saddam Hussein poses." Gary Rosenblatt edited Jewish Week. In mid-December 2002 he wrote: "Washington imminent war on Saddam Hussein is not only an opportunity to rid the world of a dangerous tyrant who presents a particularly horrific threat to Israel." He added: "when a despot announces his evil intentions, believe him. That is one of the lessons we should have learned from Hitler and the Holocaust. What is more, the Torah instructs that when your enemy seeks to kill you, kill him first. Self-defense is not permitted; it is commanded." AIPAC lobbied quietly. Executive director Howard Kohr admitted to the New York Sun in January 2003 that "quietly lobbying Congress to approve the use of force in Iraq" was one of "AIPAC successes over the past year." Jeffrey Goldberg reported in the New Yorker that "AIPAC lobbied Congress in favor of the Iraq war." In fall 2003 Senate Republicans asked AIPAC to lobby Senate Democrats to approve more war funding. AIPAC representatives talked to some Democratic senators and the money was approved. Bush spoke at AIPAC in May 2004 defending his Iraq policy. He got twenty-three standing ovations. At the 2007 AIPAC conference, when public opinion had soured, Cheney made the case for staying in Iraq and got "considerable applause" according to the Jerusalem Post. House Minority Leader John Boehner got a standing ovation when he said: "Who does not believe that failure in Iraq is not a direct threat to the state of Israel?" When Speaker Nancy Pelosi criticized the surge, many in the audience booed. Now the polls. A 2007 Gallup study based on thirteen polls since 2005 found that American Jews were significantly more opposed to the Iraq war than the general public: 77 percent opposed compared to 52 percent. Just after the war started, Columbia journalism professor Samuel Freedman reported that "a compilation of nationwide opinion polls by the Pew Research Center shows that Jews are less supportive of the Iraq war than the population at large, 52% to 62%." As the authors put it: "It would therefore be a cardinal error to attribute the war in Iraq to Jewish influence, or to blame the Jews for the war. Rather, the war was due in large part to the lobby influence, and especially its neoconservative wing. And the lobby, as we have emphasized before, is not always representative of the larger community for which it often claims to speak." this is the fact that destroys the antisemitism counter. When someone says the Iraq war was pushed by pro-Israel forces, the response is always "that is an antisemitic conspiracy theory." But look at the numbers. American Jews were more against the war than the general public. 77 percent to 52 percent. So the war was not pushed by Jewish Americans. It was pushed by a small set of organizations and neoconservatives who claim to speak for them, and who were out of step with them. That is not a Jewish conspiracy. That is a lobby that does not represent the community it claims to represent. And it sold a war that most American Jews did not want. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: The Iraq war was never supposed to be just about Iraq. It was the first step in a much bigger plan. Remove Saddam, turn Iraq into a democracy, and watch the dominoes fall across the whole region. The people who designed this plan said so publicly, and they said where the idea came from. Vice President Cheney laid it out in his speech to the VFW convention on August 26 2002, the speech that opened the campaign to sell the war. "When the gravest of threats are eliminated," he said, "the freedom-loving peoples of the region will have a chance to promote the values that can bring lasting peace... And our ability to advance the Israeli-Palestinian peace process would be enhanced." Bush said the same thing at the American Enterprise Institute on February 26 2003. "Success in Iraq could also begin a new stage for Middle Eastern peace, and set in motion progress towards a truly democratic Palestinian peace." Both men had opposed nation building before 9/11. Bush had attacked Clinton for it in the 2000 campaign. So what changed? A Wall Street Journal story in March 2003 answered that question in its headline: "President Dream: Changing Not Just Regime but a Region: A Pro-U.S., Democratic Area Is a Goal That Has Israeli and Neoconservative Roots." Charles Krauthammer said the scheme was the brainchild of Natan Sharansky, the Israeli politician whose writings impressed Bush. Israeli leaders were saying the same thing in public. Ehud Barak wrote in the New York Times in early September 2002 that "putting an end to Saddam Hussein regime will change the geopolitical landscape of the Arab world." He said it would "create an opening for forward movement on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict." Yuval Steinitz, a Likud member of the Knesset Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee, told the Christian Science Monitor in August 2002: "After Iraq is taken by U.S. troops and we see a new regime installed as in Afghanistan, and Iraqi bases become American bases, it will be very easy to pressure Syria to stop supporting terrorist organizations like Hizbullah and Islamic Jihad, to allow the Lebanese army to dismantle Hizbullah, and maybe to put an end to the Syrian occupation in Lebanon. If this happens we will really see a new Middle East." Aluf Benn reported in Ha'aretz in February 2003 that senior Israeli officers close to Sharon "paint a rosy picture of the wonderful future Israel can expect after the war. They envision a domino effect, with the fall of Saddam Hussein followed by that of Israel other enemies: Arafat, Hassan Nasrallah, Bashar Assad, the ayatollah in Iran and maybe even Muhammar Gadaffi. Along with these leaders will disappear terror and weapons of mass destruction." Ephraim Halevy, Sharon national security adviser, gave a speech in Munich in February 2003. He said: "The shock waves emerging from post-Saddam Baghdad could have wide-ranging effects in Tehran, Damascus, and in Ramallah." This was not new thinking. The 1996 Clean Break report that Feith, Perle, and Wurmser wrote for Netanyahu also called for Israel to reorder the entire Middle East. And the strategy of dual containment, which put large American forces in the Gulf to contain both Iran and Iraq, was written by Martin Indyk at WINEP in May 1993. According to Indyk Brookings colleague Kenneth Pollack, dual containment was adopted largely in response to "Israel security concerns." My analysis is this is the part that makes the whole thing click. They did not just want Saddam gone. They wanted the entire region remade. Arafat, Nasrallah, Assad, the ayatollah in Iran, Gaddafi. The list goes on. And they wanted American soldiers to do it. The Wall Street Journal headline said it had "Israeli and Neoconservative Roots." That is not me saying it. That is the Wall Street Journal. They wrote the plan down in 1996. They sold it to Bush after 9/11. And they used the American military to try to make it real. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: The war did not go the way they promised. No WMD. No democracy cascade. Iran became the main winner. The authors point out the obvious: the war was a disaster for the United States and it was not good for Israel either. The Forward reported in early 2007 that a "growing chorus" of Israeli voices were saying Israel "could find itself in more danger" now that Saddam was gone. Amatzia Baram was an Israeli expert on Iraq. He argued for Saddam ouster in prewar interviews in AIPAC Near East Report. In January 2007 he said: "If I knew then what I know today, I would not have recommended going to war, because Saddam was far less dangerous than I thought." He admitted the invasion produced "much, much more terror than I expected." Yuval Diskin, head of Shin Bet, said in February 2006: "I am not sure we wont miss Saddam." And yet the war continued, and Israel kept pushing for it to continue. Olmert spoke at AIPAC in March 2007: "Those who are concerned for Israel security... should recognize the need for American success in Iraq and responsible exit." He ended: "when America succeeds in Iraq, Israel is safer. The friends of Israel know it." Ha'aretz columnist Bradley Burston had a simple message for him: "Stay the hell out of it." Congressman Gary Ackerman said: "I am shocked. It is a very unrealistic observation. Most of us here understand that our policy has been a thorough and total disaster for the United States." Olmert had already said the same thing at the White House in November 2006: "We are very much impressed and encouraged by the stability which the great operation of America in Iraq brought to the Middle East." Then the rewriting started. David Horovitz, editor of the Jerusalem Post, wrote in March 2007 about "the false notion that Israel encouraged the US to fight the Iraq War." Shai Feldman of Brandeis told the Washington Post in summer 2006: "Israel didnt mobilize anybody over Iraq, and associating Israel with the neocons on this issue is preposterous. Israel didnt see Iraq as a danger." Martin Kramer at WINEP called any link between Israel and the war "simply a falsehood." Yossi Alpher hinted that Sharon privately warned Bush against the war. The authors checked the record and found no evidence for this. In fact Sharon own spokesman kept stressing Iraq WMD danger and Sharon told the Bush administration that postponing the attack "will not create a more convenient environment for action in the future." Olmert also hoped the lobby could help bury the Iraq Study Group recommendation that the road to Baghdad runs through Jerusalem. Ha'aretz reported in late November 2006 that Olmert "hopes the Jewish lobby can rally a Democratic majority in the new Congress to counter any diversion from the status quo on the Palestinians." My analysis is this is what victory looks like when you lose. They cannot say the war was a good idea anymore. So they say they never pushed for it. But the record is there. Netanyahu telling senators that Saddam could deliver nukes to America in suitcases. Peres on CNN. Sharon calling Iraq "the greatest danger facing Israel." The CBS headline "Israel to US: Don't Delay Iraq Attack." The Israel Project memo telling them to hide it. The Knesset report saying the intelligence was false. Then they look you in the eye and say it was never about Israel. Kennedy said victory has a thousand fathers but defeat is an orphan. Iraq was a defeat. So now everyone is running from it. But the documents do not run. They stay right where they are. Source: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy, 2007, a book written by John Mearsheimer and Stephen Walt # Israel # Zionist # MiddleEast # HumanRights # Palestine

ARCHIVE: Israel took the Golan Heights from Syria in the 1967 war. It drove eighty thousand Syrians from their homes. Israeli law was extended over the territory in 1981, in what was essentially a de facto annexation. There are now about eighteen thousand Jewish settlers living there in thirty-two settlements and one city. For a while, Israeli leaders accepted the idea of giving it back. In 1994 Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin agreed in principle to return all of the Golan Heights to Syria in return for full normalization of relations. The "Rabin deposit" meant Israel would withdraw to the June 4 1967 border, and Syria would end all support for Hezbollah, Hamas, and Islamic Jihad. Rabin was assassinated a year later, but Shimon Peres and Benjamin Netanyahu remained committed in principle. Ehud Barak was also willing to give back virtually all of the Golan, though he would not commit to the full 1967 border. In fall 1999 Clinton thought he had a deal. At Barak strong urging he brought both sides to Shepherdstown, West Virginia in early January 2000. But Barak suddenly became inflexible. Israeli public opinion was cool to giving the Golan back, so he slowed the process to look tough. The talks collapsed. Dennis Ross, Clinton chief Middle East negotiator, said later: "If not for Barak cold feet, there might have been a deal in January 2000." A follow-up meeting in Geneva went nowhere because Assad no longer trusted Barak. Clinton clearly blamed Israel, not Syria, for the collapse. Then Ariel Sharon became prime minister in February 2001. He had no intention of giving back the Golan. "What was offered back then," he said, "in my wildest imagination, I would not have considered." His successor Ehud Olmert made it clear: "the Golan Heights will remain in our hands forever." The Israeli public agrees. Now, already in mid November, some new developments took place already, not so much in Rojava but in other parts in Kurdistan. We will also report about it here. ----------------------------------------------------------------- Monthly higlights, October 2026 ----------------------------------------------------------------- # FORMER SDF DIVISIONS COMPLETE TRAINING The former SDF units are undergoing an standardized education in Damascus to formalize the integration in the ministry of defense as agreed in the integration talks. On October the main forces completed of what became the Hasakah liwa (division) completed their training and the Kobane division started it. # NEGOTIATIONS ARE ONGOING OF A THIRD DIVISION IN AFRIN SDF fighters who returned after the education mentioned how the education focused on what the trainers presented as "islamic values" more than in the technical aspect of the military forces. # VIOLENCE AGAINST IDP With the ongoing return of Kurdish IDPs to their homes, the violence against them continues to increase. IDPs returning to Serekaniye and Afrin are facing violent attacks from mobs organized under banners of "arab tribes". The houses where they return are often looted and destroyed, facing very difficult conditions on arrival. Many of this attacks can be traced to armed groups connected to the SNA, the turkish backed militias that in theory merged into the Syrian army. At the end of October Kurdish refugees returning to Gire Spi faced heavy violence, with attackers beating kurdish IDPs and burning their cars on arrival. # INCREASING TENSIONS IN HASAKAH The neighborhood of Ghuwayran, that hosts the prisons of ISIS fighters and a majority of Arab population, has been a friction point for tensions between Kurdish and Arab populations. Demonstrations to demand that education is held in Kurdish language faced counter-demonstration from Arab population, with threatening actions against Kurdish people often being overlooked if not directly encourage by government forces. # SYRIA FLOODS On October heavy rains in Syria led to floods in Aleppo, Raqqa, Deir ez-Zor, Hasakah, Hama, Homs and Latakia governorates. At least 5 people lost their live due to the floods and The Syrian Civil Defense has carried out more than 300 emergency responses. Homes and refugee camps in Raqqa and Deir Ezzor had to be evacuated. Roads and bridges suffered damages from the floods, as well as power lines and other logistical infrastructure like fiber-optic cable. These floods deepened the humanitarian crisis in Syria, that together with increasing living costs are deepening the hardships that many families across Syria are suffering. # ISREAL ADVANCES IN SOUTHERN SYRIA Israel has been intensifying their operation is Southern Syria, establishing checkpoints and arresting farmers in the Quneitra region. Together with increasing negotiations and military support to the Druze areas of Swueida, circulating reports are hinting at potential operations being lined out on Israel headquarters to extend their influence on Syria. A coordinated advance of Druze forces and IDF in southern Syria could dramatically increase tensions between both countries. ----------------------------------------------------------------- LATE DEVELOPMENTS IN KURDISTAN # CHANGING CONDITIONS OF ABDULLAH ÖCALAN Abdullah Öcalan has been transferred from his cell in Imrali prison to a newly build compound inside the prison walls. The compound serves as an office were öcalan can receive visits of politicians, journalists and state representatives, and is presented as a step on the ongoing peace negotiations. Öcalan is considered now in house arrest in the new compound, from where he is expected to have a critical role in the negotiation process between the Kurdish Liberation Movement and the Turkish State. # GOVERNMENT CRISIS IN KRG Since the election of late 2024, originally planned for 2022 but repeatedly postponed over dispute on the election law, KRG (Kurdish Regional Government) couldn't consolidate a government. After KDP (Kurdish Democratic Party) forced the creation of a unilateral government, PUK (Patriotic Union of Kurdistan) withdraw from the parliament and seek negotiations with Baghdad aiming to access the budget of the regions in their control separated from the rest of KRG. The already tense political situation of Iraq, impacted also by the Iran war and with ongoing debates on other Kurdish disputed areas like Sinjar and Kirkuk, is also affected by the US movements withdrawing it's military forces from the region. Negotiations to solve the current crisis are ongoing, with several Kurdish parties working to mitigate tensions and find some consensus agreements. # CLASHES IN ROJHILAT As tensions between US and Iran continue increasing, with looming threats of intensified return of hostilities beyond what took place until now, clashes between IRGC forces and YRK guerrillas of the Kurdish Liberation Movement are intensifying. After several artillery and drone attacks of IRGC into guerrilla territories, on the beginning of November PJAK announced an action into a military headquarter of IRGC where guerrillas took control of the station for a few hours, destroying weapons an military equipment. PJAK announced the identity of a guerrilla fighter who lost his life on an ambush by IRGC forces, remarking that PJAK is only carrying out defensive operations and won't act on behalf of any foreign forces ----------------------------------------------------------------- Evaluation The negotiations for the integration process of Rojava into the new Syrian State navigated the most pressing issues to avoid a military conflict, but left many issues unresolved, hoping for further agreements and negotiations. Without the urgency that military escalation brings, remaining tensions are being the source of conflicts where civilian organizations struggle on daily basis in the streets. Subsuming military tensions opened space for civil organizing, but the new government of Damascus and it's strong alliance with Turkey leaves very few space for democratic developments. Even with millionary investments of Arab countries and European powers, the economical situation is not improving for many Syrians. New companies and economic institutions are hording the resources that come from abroad, while prices are skyrocketing and many people struggle to meet their basic financial needs. Nearing the two years since Bashar al-Assad left the country, the situation in Syria is far away from stable. The transitional government secured the lifting of sanctions imposed on Syria, its institutions and individuals. It rebuilt international relations through partnerships with Turkiye, Qatar and Saudi Arabia, closer ties with Arab and Muslim countries, and improved relations with the United States, Britain and the European Union, while preserving ties with Russia. Internally, massacres against Alawite population on coastal regions, clashes against Druze militias and harsh negotiations with the Kurdish forces allowed a frame of national unity based on a constrained repression of ethnic minorities, denying claims for a federal Syria more autonomy for ethnic diversity. For the Kurdish people, the relevant processes taking place in Bakur and Rojhilat (PKK peace negotiations on Turkey and US/Israel war on Iran) are having heavy influence on the situation in Rojava. The extraordinary project of over a decade long autonomy is still alive in the imaginary of the people, but the dismantlement of the revolutionary institutions and the turmoil of the region create important difficulties to continue developing the revolutionary project. National unity among the Kurdish regions is becoming a tangible reality as never before, but it also comes with big challenges. Regional instability can still change the course of history in any direction, with events of unexpected dimensions developing every day. Still, the Kurdish question is now a reality being discussed in all four parts of Kurdistan, and extraordinary steps and sacrifices made possible for Kurdish people to overcome the annihilation that brought their existence to the verge of extinction. For us, revolutionary anarchist from many places, their struggle is an example of resistance and determination against all odds. Rojava has become a beacon of hope, bringing important lessons not only about what a revolution needs, but also how to navigate the consequences and reactions that revolutionary transformations bring.
